note:
Doctor: Good morning. I have you down as a 71-year-old male here for your six-month visit for low-risk prostate cancer on active surveillance. How have you been feeling?
Patient: Pretty good, honestly. I get up once at night to urinate and the stream is a little slow, but that has been the same for a long time.
Doctor: Any burning when you urinate, blood in the urine, or pain in your back or hips?
Patient: No burning, no blood in the urine, and no bone pain.
Doctor: Any weight loss or new fatigue?
Patient: No, my weight has been steady and I feel fine.
Doctor: Good. Let me go over your medicines. You take tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily for the urine flow and amlodipine 5 mg daily for your hypertension, right?
Patient: Yes. My home readings have been running higher lately, around one fifty over ninety.
Doctor: Okay. And you are still allergic to penicillin, correct? You broke out in hives with it years ago.
Patient: That's right, hives all over.
Doctor: Noted. Your vitals today are blood pressure 152/90, heart rate 76, temperature 36.8 Celsius, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. On exam your abdomen is soft and nontender, and there is no bone tenderness over the spine. On rectal exam the prostate is mildly enlarged and smooth, with no new nodules. Your PSA today is 5.8, up from 4.6 a year ago, and your MRI from last month shows a PI-RADS 4 lesion in the left peripheral zone that was not there before.
Patient: Does that mean the cancer is getting worse?
Doctor: It means we need tissue to find out. I would like to do a repeat targeted biopsy. Because of your penicillin allergy, I will give you ciprofloxacin 500 mg once, one hour before the biopsy, to prevent infection, and I will avoid any penicillin-type antibiotic.
Doctor: Your blood pressure is above goal, so I am increasing amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily. Keep taking tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. We will recheck your blood pressure in four weeks. I want to see you two weeks after the biopsy results, and if everything is stable we will go back to PSA every six months.
Patient: Okay, I understand. I will schedule the biopsy today.
summary: A 71-year-old male with low-risk prostate cancer on active surveillance came for a six-month visit, reporting a slow stream and getting up once at night but no burning, blood in the urine, bone pain, weight loss or new fatigue. He has hypertension with higher home readings and a penicillin allergy with hives. Blood pressure was 152/90, the prostate was mildly enlarged without nodules, and PSA rose to 5.8 from 4.6 with a new PI-RADS 4 lesion on MRI. The plan is a repeat targeted biopsy with ciprofloxacin prophylaxis instead of a penicillin-type antibiotic, amlodipine increased to 10 mg daily, tamsulosin continued, and follow-up two weeks after the biopsy results.

Rectal exam: prostate mildly enlarged and smooth, no new nodules. PSA 5.8, up from 4.6 a year ago. MRI last month shows a new PI-RADS 4 lesion in the left peripheral zone.
soap.assessment: Low-risk prostate cancer on active surveillance with a rising PSA and a new PI-RADS 4 lesion, needing tissue confirmation. Hypertension above goal. Penicillin allergy documented.

Ciprofloxacin 500 mg once, one hour before the biopsy, for infection prophylaxis; avoid penicillin-type antibiotics given the allergy
Increase amlodipine from 5 mg to 10 mg daily
Continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily
Recheck blood pressure in four weeks
Follow up two weeks after the biopsy results; if stable, return to PSA every six months

note: This is a dictation for a urology clinic follow-up visit on a 60-year-old male with benign prostatic hyperplasia and lower urinary tract symptoms. He returned from a three week trip to India about ten days ago and says his urinary symptoms got worse during the long flight and have stayed bad since. He reports a weak stream, hesitancy, a feeling of incomplete emptying, urgency, and getting up three times a night. He denies burning with urination. He denies gross blood in the urine, denies fever, and denies flank pain. He had a short episode of traveler's diarrhea while abroad that resolved on its own. He took no antibiotics for it. He took pseudoephedrine for nasal congestion during the flight and for a few days afterward. He currently takes tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily and has no known drug allergies. Blood pressure today is 134 over 82, heart rate 72, and temperature 36.9 Celsius. The abdomen is soft, the suprapubic area is not distended or tender, and there is no costovertebral angle tenderness. Rectal exam shows a smooth, symmetric, enlarged prostate, approximately 50 grams, without nodules. Urinalysis today is negative for nitrite, leukocyte esterase and blood. Bladder scan shows a post void residual of 110 milliliters, correction, 140 milliliters. His symptom score is 18, which is moderately severe. PSA is 2.1 and stable compared with last year. Impression is one, benign prostatic hyperplasia with worsening lower urinary tract symptoms, likely aggravated by pseudoephedrine and dehydration during travel, and two, a mildly elevated post void residual without frank retention. Plan is to stop pseudoephedrine and avoid over the counter decongestants, to start finasteride 5 mg once daily, to continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg once daily, to send a urine culture because of his recent travel, to encourage normal fluid intake, and to repeat the symptom score and bladder scan in three months. He should return sooner or go to the emergency department if he cannot urinate, develops fever, or sees blood in the urine. End of dictation.
summary: A 60-year-old male with benign prostatic hyperplasia returned from a three week trip to India with worsening weak stream, hesitancy, incomplete emptying, urgency and getting up three times a night, but no burning, gross blood in the urine, fever or flank pain. He took pseudoephedrine during and after the flight and had a self-limited episode of traveler's diarrhea. Examination showed a smooth enlarged prostate, a negative urinalysis, a post void residual of 140 milliliters and a stable PSA of 2.1. The impression is worsening lower urinary tract symptoms aggravated by pseudoephedrine and dehydration. Pseudoephedrine is stopped, finasteride is started with tamsulosin continued, a urine culture is sent, and he will be reassessed in three months.

note:
Telephone visit (audio only) for a 21-year-old male referred to gastroenterology for progressive dysphagia. Identity was confirmed and verbal consent for a phone visit was obtained; he is at home.

HPI: About 6 months of difficulty swallowing solid foods that has gradually worsened. Bread and meat feel like they stick in the lower chest behind the breastbone, and he now eats slowly and drinks water with every bite to get food down. Two weeks ago a piece of chicken stuck for about 20 minutes before it passed on its own. He has trouble only with solids and has no trouble swallowing liquids. He also has heartburn once or twice a week. He denies weight loss, pain with swallowing, vomiting blood, black stools, chest pain, and fever. He has no hoarseness and no cough with meals.

History: Asthma and eczema since childhood. No known drug allergies. Current medications are an albuterol inhaler as needed and famotidine 20 mg as needed, which helps very little. Current tobacco use: he smokes about half a pack of cigarettes a day and has for the past 3 years.

Home-reported data: Home pulse 70 and temperature 36.8 Celsius. Weight 172 lb on his home scale, unchanged over 6 months. Labs from his primary care visit last month, read to me from the patient portal: hemoglobin 14.8, white blood cell count 7.4, and normal ferritin.

Exam: Limited to what can be assessed by phone. He speaks in full sentences, his voice is clear without hoarseness, and he does not sound short of breath. No physical exam was performed.

Impression: Progressive dysphagia to solids with one food impaction in a young patient with asthma and eczema. Eosinophilic esophagitis is the leading working diagnosis, and he also has intermittent heartburn.

Orders and advice: Schedule an EGD with esophageal biopsies within 2 weeks. Stop famotidine and start omeprazole 40 mg once daily, 30 minutes before breakfast, for 8 weeks. Eat soft, moist foods, cut food into small pieces, chew thoroughly, and avoid eating when rushed. Go to the emergency department if food is stuck for more than an hour or if he cannot swallow his saliva. Counseled on stopping smoking and offered cessation support; he is not ready to quit right now. Telephone follow-up after the EGD.

He denies weight loss, pain with swallowing, vomiting blood, black stools, chest pain, fever, hoarseness and cough with meals. He has asthma and eczema, and labs from last month showed hemoglobin 14.8 and a white count of 7.4. The impression is progressive dysphagia, with eosinophilic esophagitis as the leading working diagnosis. Famotidine is stopped and omeprazole is started, an EGD with esophageal biopsies is planned within two weeks, and he received food-impaction precautions and smoking cessation counseling.

note:
Hospital day 2 progress note for a 43-year-old male with epilepsy who was admitted to the ward after a breakthrough seizure. He has had no further seizures overnight and continues levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. This morning the nurse noticed that both of his eyes were red with watery discharge. His brother, who is his caregiver and stayed overnight at the bedside, reports that the eyes were crusted shut when the patient woke up and that the patient has had a runny nose for the past three days. The patient himself says his eyes feel gritty. He denies eye pain, denies blurred vision, and denies sensitivity to light. He has no fever and does not wear contact lenses.

Temperature is 37.0 Celsius, heart rate 78, blood pressure 124/78, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. He is alert and comfortable. There is redness of the conjunctivae in both eyes with clear watery discharge and mild eyelid swelling. Pupils are equal and reactive, visual acuity is grossly intact, and the corneas look clear. There is a small tender preauricular lymph node on the right. The nasal mucosa is mildly red with clear rhinorrhea, and the throat is clear.

My impression is acute viral conjunctivitis, likely adenoviral. I do not think antibiotic drops are needed. The plan is artificial tears, one drop in each eye four times daily as needed, cool compresses, and contact precautions with strict hand washing and separate towels while he is on the ward. Continue levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily. His brother was taught the hand hygiene steps. Ask ophthalmology to see him if he develops eye pain, vision change, or no improvement within a week.
summary: A 43-year-old male with epilepsy, on hospital day 2 after a breakthrough seizure, developed red eyes with watery discharge, crusting, a gritty feeling and a runny nose for three days, with part of the history given by his brother who is his caregiver. He denies eye pain, blurred vision and sensitivity to light and has no fever. Examination showed bilateral conjunctival redness with clear watery discharge, mild eyelid swelling and a small tender right preauricular node, with intact visual acuity. The impression is acute viral conjunctivitis, likely adenoviral. He will use artificial tears and cool compresses with contact precautions, continue levetiracetam, and have ophthalmology review if symptoms worsen.

note:
Telehealth video visit, dermatology follow-up. The patient is a 70-year-old male at home on a secure video connection; verbal consent for the virtual visit was obtained.

Reason for visit: Rough, scaly spots on the scalp, forehead and backs of the hands that have been present for several months, consistent with his known actinic keratoses.

History: He says the spots feel rough and occasionally itch, and a few look more red than before. He denies bleeding, pain, rapid growth, and open sores. He was hospitalized 3 weeks ago for pneumonia and went home after 4 days; he finished his antibiotic course. He has no fever and no cough now, but still tires easily. He has hypertension and hyperlipidemia and takes lisinopril 10 mg daily, atorvastatin 20 mg daily, and aspirin 81 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies. He worked outdoors for most of his life and rarely used sunscreen.

Home measurements today: blood pressure 128/76, pulse 70, temperature 36.7 Celsius. From his discharge paperwork he read that the chest x-ray showed a right lower lobe infiltrate and the white blood cell count was 8.4 at discharge.

Video exam, limited: Lighting was good and I reviewed photographs he uploaded. There are multiple 3 to 6 mm erythematous scaly macules and papules over the scalp and forehead, and several on the dorsal hands. No ulceration, bleeding, or nodular lesion is visible. He appears comfortable and speaks in full sentences.

Impression: Multiple actinic keratoses of the scalp, forehead and hands. Recent pneumonia, recovering. Hypertension controlled by home readings.

Orders and advice: Because he is still recovering from his hospitalization, in-office cryotherapy will be deferred. Start fluorouracil 5% cream, thin layer to the forehead and scalp twice daily for 3 weeks, and he was told to expect redness, crusting and irritation. Daily sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher and a wide-brimmed hat. Continue current medications. In-person visit in 4 weeks for a total body skin exam, cryotherapy of persistent lesions, and biopsy of anything suspicious. Contact the clinic sooner for bleeding, ulceration, rapid growth, or return of fever. Follow up with his primary care clinician about the pneumonia.

The spots are rough and occasionally itchy, and he denies bleeding, pain, rapid growth, open sores, fever and cough. Home blood pressure was 128/76, and video exam showed multiple scaly erythematous macules and papules on the scalp, forehead and dorsal hands without ulceration. The impression is multiple actinic keratoses, recovering pneumonia and controlled hypertension. Cryotherapy is deferred, fluorouracil 5% cream is started, sun protection is advised, and an in-person skin exam is planned in four weeks.

note:
Hospital day 2 progress note for an 83-year-old male admitted yesterday after a syncopal episode. Yesterday afternoon, while standing up from a chair after lunch, he felt lightheaded, his vision grayed out, and he lost consciousness for less than a minute according to a witness. He fell but did not seem to strike his head, and he was alert within a minute. He denies chest pain, palpitations, and shortness of breath before the event. There was no seizure activity, no tongue biting, and no incontinence. He admits to a poor appetite and low fluid intake for several days. Past history includes atrial fibrillation, hypertension, and benign prostatic hyperplasia. Home medications are apixaban 5 mg twice daily, metoprolol succinate 100 mg daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, and tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily. He has no known drug allergies.

Overnight there were no events. Telemetry shows atrial fibrillation with controlled rates between 58 and 88 and no pauses longer than 2 seconds or ventricular tachycardia. Troponin was negative twice. CT head on admission showed no hemorrhage. Echocardiogram shows an ejection fraction of 55% with mild aortic sclerosis and no stenosis. Today temperature is 36.8 Celsius, heart rate 70, respiratory rate 16, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. Orthostatic blood pressures were 138/80 supine and 104/62 after 3 minutes standing, with lightheadedness on standing. On exam he is alert and his mucous membranes are dry. The rhythm is irregularly irregular with a soft systolic murmur, the lungs are clear, there is no scalp hematoma or bruising, and the neurologic exam is nonfocal. Hemoglobin is 12.9 and stable, creatinine is 1.3 up from a baseline of 1.0, sodium 138 and potassium 4.2.

My impression is that the syncope is most consistent with orthostatic hypotension from volume depletion, compounded by his antihypertensives and tamsulosin. Arrhythmic or structural causes are less likely given the telemetry and echocardiogram. His atrial fibrillation is rate controlled. He remains on apixaban with no bleeding and a negative head CT.

For today, give a 500 mL bolus of normal saline, then encourage oral fluids. Stop lisinopril. Decrease metoprolol succinate from 100 mg to 50 mg daily. Continue tamsulosin 0.4 mg daily, taken at bedtime, with slow position changes. Continue apixaban 5 mg twice daily; no dose reduction is needed at this time. Fall precautions and a physical therapy evaluation. Repeat orthostatic blood pressures and a basic metabolic panel tomorrow morning. Anticipate discharge tomorrow if the orthostatics improve, with primary care and cardiology follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks.
summary: An 83-year-old male on apixaban for atrial fibrillation was admitted after syncope on standing, preceded by lightheadedness and graying of vision, with no chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath or seizure features. Orthostatic blood pressures fell from 138/80 supine to 104/62 standing, telemetry showed rate-controlled atrial fibrillation without pauses, troponin was negative, head CT showed no hemorrhage, and creatinine was 1.3. The impression is orthostatic hypotension from volume depletion compounded by antihypertensives and tamsulosin. He receives a normal saline bolus, lisinopril is stopped, metoprolol succinate is reduced to 50 mg daily, and apixaban continues with fall precautions and physical therapy.

soap.subjective: 83-year-old male, hospital day 2 after syncope. note:
79-year-old male seen in the gastroenterology clinic for heartburn that has not responded to treatment over the past 6 months. He describes a burning feeling behind the breastbone and a sour taste in his mouth almost every day, worse after dinner and when lying flat, with frequent night waking. He denies trouble swallowing, food sticking, vomiting, black stools, blood in his stool, and weight loss. He has been taking omeprazole 20 mg once daily, but when asked to show how he takes it, he swallows it with dinner rather than before a meal, and he sometimes skips it when he forgets. He also chews calcium carbonate tablets several times a day for relief and takes ibuprofen as needed for knee pain, which he calls his arthritis pills. He has limited health literacy and says he has trouble reading the labels on his bottles; his daughter fills a pill box for him on Sundays. His other history is hypertension, treated with amlodipine 5 mg once daily.

Today his blood pressure is 136/78, heart rate 74, and weight 182 lb, which is stable. He is comfortable, and the abdomen is soft and nontender without masses. Hemoglobin last week was 13.6, which is normal. I used plain language and teach-back throughout the visit and drew a simple picture schedule; at the end he could say back that the stomach pill goes before breakfast.

My impression is refractory GERD, likely worsened by incorrect timing of omeprazole and regular ibuprofen use. He has no alarm features, but given his age and persistent symptoms I recommend an EGD. I am increasing omeprazole to 40 mg once daily, taken 30 minutes before breakfast. He will stop ibuprofen and use acetaminophen 500 mg every 6 hours as needed for knee pain, no more than 4 doses a day. Continue amlodipine 5 mg once daily, and use calcium carbonate only as needed. Raise the head of the bed and avoid eating within 3 hours of bedtime. A large-print picture medication chart was given to him and his daughter. The EGD will be scheduled in 4 weeks, with follow-up in 8 weeks.

Doctor: Hello. I understand you are a 36-year-old female here about a rash after a tick bite?
Patient: Yes. I found a tick on the back of my knee about ten days ago after hiking in the woods. It was attached for a day, I think. Then four days ago a red patch showed up there and it keeps getting bigger.
Doctor: Does it itch or hurt?
Patient: Not really, it is just warm. I have had a mild headache and I feel a bit tired.
Doctor: Any fever, stiff neck, facial drooping, joint swelling, or palpitations?
Patient: No fever, no stiff neck, my face feels normal, and my joints are fine. No racing heart either.
Doctor: Any allergies to medicines? Are you pregnant or breastfeeding?
Patient: No allergies, and no, neither.
Doctor: Good. Your temperature is 36.9 Celsius, heart rate 74, and blood pressure 118 over 74. Behind your right knee there is a round red patch about 10 centimeters across with a slightly clearer center. It is flat and not tender. You have no other rashes, your joints are not swollen, your face is symmetric, and your heart sounds regular.
Patient: So what is it?
Doctor: This is a typical erythema migrans rash, which means early Lyme disease. The rash is diagnostic, so I do not need a blood test today. I am starting doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for ten days. Take it with food and a full glass of water, and use sunscreen because it can make you sun sensitive.
Patient: Should I watch for anything?
Doctor: Yes. Call us or come back if you develop a fever, stiff neck, facial weakness, joint swelling, or a racing heartbeat. Otherwise, we will see you in two weeks to make sure the rash is clearing.

She has a mild headache and feels tired, but denies fever, stiff neck, facial drooping, joint swelling and racing heart, and she has no medication allergies. Vital signs were normal, and the examination showed a flat, nontender round red patch about 10 centimeters across with central clearing. The diagnosis is early Lyme disease with typical erythema migrans, and no blood test is needed. She is started on doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for ten days with return precautions and follow-up in two weeks.

Telephone visit (audio only) to review recent results with a 52-year-old male who has primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia. Identity was verified, verbal consent was given, and he is at home.

History: Hypercalcemia was found on routine labs and confirmed on repeat testing. He reports mild fatigue and occasional constipation. He denies kidney stones, bone pain, abdominal pain, excessive thirst, and confusion. He has hypertension and has taken hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg daily for several years. He takes no other regular medications. His home blood pressure cuff read 142/88 this morning with a pulse of 70.

Results reviewed: Calcium 11.6 mg/dL, PTH 112 pg/mL (elevated), 25-hydroxy vitamin D 34 ng/mL, and creatinine 0.9 mg/dL. A DEXA scan showed a T-score of -2.6 at the distal one-third radius.

Exam: None by phone. He speaks in full sentences and is alert and oriented.

Impression: Primary hyperparathyroidism with hypercalcemia. The calcium level and the T-score both meet criteria to recommend surgery. Thiazide diuretics can raise calcium and are not ideal here.

Orders and advice: Stop hydrochlorothiazide and start amlodipine 5 mg daily for his blood pressure. Order a neck ultrasound and a sestamibi scan, and refer to endocrine surgery for parathyroidectomy. Drink at least 2 liters of fluid daily. Repeat calcium and creatinine in 2 weeks. Phone follow-up after the imaging and surgical consultation. Go to the emergency department for severe abdominal pain, confusion, or sudden severe flank pain.

Doctor: Good afternoon. I see you are a 94-year-old male, here about swelling in your ankles, and you also wanted to talk about your wishes for future care. Is that right?
Patient: Yes. My ankles have been puffy this week, and I would like to get my paperwork in order.
Doctor: Let's start with the ankles. Any cough, fever, chest pain, or trouble lying flat?
Patient: No cough, no fever, no chest pain, and I sleep fine. I do get a little winded on the stairs.
Doctor: You still work the overnight shifts at the community center, right? How does that affect your pills?
Patient: Three or four nights a week, and my schedule changes all the time. On those days I never know if it is morning or night, so I skip the water pill so I am not running to the bathroom at work.
Doctor: That explains it. Your weight today is 168 pounds, up four from your last visit. Blood pressure is 128 over 70, heart rate 68, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. I hear a few crackles at the bases, and there is mild pitting edema in both ankles. Your creatinine from today's blood test is 1.4, close to your baseline.
Doctor: You have heart failure, chronic kidney disease, and high blood pressure. For the fluid, I am increasing your furosemide from 20 mg to 40 mg once daily. Take it when you wake up, whatever time that is, and label your pill box wake-up and bedtime instead of morning and evening. Keep taking lisinopril 10 mg daily, and we will recheck your blood work in one week.
Patient: Okay, that makes sense.
Doctor: Now about your wishes. If your heart or kidneys got much worse, what matters most to you?
Patient: Staying in my own home and staying independent. I do not want to be on machines.
Doctor: Would you want CPR if your heart stopped?
Patient: No. And no breathing tube. But I would go to the hospital for something fixable, like pneumonia.
Doctor: I will document that as do not resuscitate and do not intubate, with hospitalization for treatable problems. Who should speak for you if you cannot?
Patient: My niece. She knows what I want.
Doctor: Good. We will complete the health care proxy form and the portable medical order form today and give copies to you and your niece. You can change your mind at any time. Please follow up with your primary care doctor in one week for the repeat labs and bring these forms with you.
Patient: I will. Thank you for listening.
